introduction-the-importance-of-communica.core: Silence during an incident creates chaos: customers assume the worst, support is flooded and executives interrupt engineers. Proactive, regular communication controls the narrative and protects the responders.

first_principles.problem: The team is focused on fixing things, nobody posts an update for an hour, and social media fills the vacuum with speculation.
truths: People fill information gaps with assumptions.
derivation: **Acknowledge** quickly, even before knowing the cause.
Tailor to the **audience**: customers, execs, support.
Use a **status page** as the single source of truth.

analogy.title: A pilot's announcements during turbulence
analogy.story: 'We're experiencing turbulence, please stay seated, next update in 10 minutes' calms the whole cabin.
analogy.breaks: Over-communicating minor issues causes alert fatigue among customers.

example.title: Silence vs cadence
flow: Cadence: first post in 5 min, updates every 30 min

check.q: Why communicate before you know the root cause?
check.a: Acknowledging the issue and committing to updates prevents speculation and floods of inbound questions.

the-single-source-of-truth-status-pages.core: A status page, hosted independently of your infrastructure, shows component health and incident updates, and lets customers subscribe. It's the canonical public source during incidents.

first_principles.problem: The status page runs on the same infrastructure that's down, so it's down too.
truths: Communication channels must survive the outage.
Customers need one place to check.
derivation: **Link** it from the app, support and social.

analogy.title: An emergency broadcast station on backup power
analogy.story: When the city's power fails, it still broadcasts.
analogy.breaks: An automated status page can mislead if its checks are wrong, so have humans confirm major incidents.

example.title: Status page components
example.outcome: a reliable public source of truth.

check.q: Why must a status page be hosted separately from your main infrastructure?
check.a: So it stays available when your main systems are down.

writing-effective-public-updates.core: A good update says what's affected, what users experience, what you're doing and when the next update comes, in plain, honest, non-technical language without speculative causes or ETAs you can't keep.

first_principles.problem: Updates like 'investigating elevated 5xx on the ingress tier' confuse customers, and promised ETAs keep slipping.
truths: Customers care about impact, not internals.
derivation: Give a **next update time**, not a fix ETA.
Stay **honest and empathetic**; avoid blame and jargon.

analogy.title: A train announcement done right
analogy.story: 'Trains to the airport are delayed due to a signal fault. Next update in 15 minutes.' Clear, honest, actionable.
analogy.breaks: Legal sensitivity (security incidents) may limit details, so coordinate with legal.

example.title: Bad vs good update

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Customers understand and trust the updates.

code.text:
✗ "Elevated error rates on ingress-nginx in use1. Fix ETA 10 min."
✓ "Some customers can't complete checkout. Our team is actively working on it.
   We'll post another update by 14:30 UTC."

example.outcome: updates that inform without confusing or over-promising.

check.q: Why promise a 'next update time' instead of a fix ETA?
check.a: Fix times are uncertain, while update times are always within your control to keep.

executive-briefings-communicating-upward.core: Executives need business impact, the risks and decisions needed, and the expected path. They don't need technical detail. Use a structured, short briefing (BLUF: bottom line up front) on a cadence, delivered by the Liaison.

first_principles.problem: Executives join the engineering channel asking 'what's going on?' and distract the responders.
derivation: Start with the **bottom line**: impact + status.
Give the **business effect**: customers, revenue, regulatory.
State **decisions needed** (e.g. approve a failover with data risk).

analogy.title: A military situation report (SITREP)
analogy.story: Short, structured, the most important information first.
analogy.breaks: Executives may still need some technical context to make risky decisions, so offer it on request.

example.title: An exec briefing

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A fast decision, and the engineers aren't interrupted.

code.text:
BLUF: Checkout down for ~30% of EU users since 13:50. Mitigation in progress, partial recovery.
Impact: ~€40k/hour revenue; no data loss.
Decision needed: approve failover to us-east (adds latency for EU).
Next update: 14:30.

example.outcome: leadership informed and enabled to decide.

check.q: What does BLUF stand for, and why use it for executive updates?
check.a: Bottom Line Up Front. Executives get the essential impact and status immediately.

customer-notification-logic-when-to-shou.core: Not every glitch deserves a broadcast. Define criteria (severity, number of customers affected, duration, data or security impact, contractual SLAs) for status page posts, targeted emails and full announcements.

first_principles.problem: Emailing every customer about a 2-minute blip trains them to ignore messages, while a real breach notification gets lost.

analogy.title: The boy who cried wolf
analogy.story: Shout about everything and nobody listens when the wolf really comes.
analogy.breaks: Enterprise contracts may require notifying specific customers regardless of your general policy.

example.title: A notification matrix
flow: SEV1 global → status + email all + postmortem

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Customers pay attention when you do write.

example.outcome: notifications that are proportionate and trusted.

check.q: Why not email all customers about every incident?
check.a: Over-notification trains customers to ignore messages, which reduces the impact of important ones.
